Verses 1-9

Introduction to the Sūrah:

This sūrah encompasses discussions about the mockery of the disbelievers towards the Prophet. They accused him of madness and claimed that the Noble Qur’an was the rambling of a madman. In response, the sūrah ofers consolation to the Prophet, commanding him to remain patient, steadfast, and forgiving towards them. It aims to uplift his noble spirit, while also serving as a warning and glad tidings.

The sūrah is M eccan, as indicated by its verses. There is a report in alM ajma’, from al-Ḥasan, that excludes the verse, “Certainly W e have given you the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur’an” (15:87) and “Even as W e sent down on the dividers, who reduced the Qur’an into pieces” (15:90).

Further details will follow.

The sūrah also includes the divine instruction: “So proclaim what you have been commanded, and turn away from the polytheists.” This verse aligns with historical accounts stating that the Prophet was discreet about his mission for the frst three, four, or fve years due to the difculties he faced. He would only invite specifc individuals whom he hoped would embrace faith, doing so in secrecy, until his Lord permitted him to publicly announce his mission.

Supporting this, there are narrations from both Shia and Sunni sources confrming that the Prophet kept his mission secret in the initial years, not revealing it to the public until the revelation of “So proclaim what you have been commanded, and turn away from the polytheists. Indeed, We will sufce you against the deriders.” After this revelation, he came forth and openly invited people to his mission. Therefore, the sūrah is Meccan and was revealed at the beginning of the public call to faith.

Among the profound Qur’anic verses in this sūrah are: “And there is not a thing but its treasuries are with Us” (15:21), and “Indeed, W e have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, W e will preserve it” (15:9).

Commentary:

(15:1) Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the signs of the Book and a manifest Qur’an.

This refers to the noble Qur’anic verses. The term “the Book” in this context means the Qur’an. The indefnite article used for the Qur’an signifes its grandeur and majesty. Additionally, the word “these” in the phrase

points to something far-of, thereby emphasizing its exalted status.

The meaning is as follows: “These are the elevated verses, of high standing, which We have revealed to you—verses from the divine Book and from

a Qur’an of great signifcance that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This is contrary to the claims made by the disbelievers, who accuse

you of madness and mock the words of God.”

It is also possible that the term “the Book” refers to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), as the Qur’an originates from it. The Almighty says, “This is indeed a noble Qur’an in a guarded Book”1 (alWaqi’ah:77-78). He also says, “Indeed it is a glorious Quran, in a preserved tablet” (al-Burūj:21-22).

Therefore, the phrase “These are the signs of the Book and a manifest Qur’an” serves as a summary of the verse, “By the manifest Book:

We have made it into an Arabic Qur’an so that you may apply reason”

(al-Zukhrūf:1-3).

(15:2) Much will the faithless wish that they had been Muslims.

This verse serves as a precursor to what they will subsequently assert

1 Or, “Preserved Tablet.” (Ed.)

when they say to the Prophet: “O you, to whom the reminder has been sent down, you are indeed crazy” (15:6). This indicates their impending regret over their current state of disbelief, and their yearning for Islam for the sake of God and faith in His Book, at a time when there will be no avenue for them to achieve this.

Regarding the phrase: “M uch will the faithless wish,” what is intended is the sentiment of longing, not an unqualifed fondness or love. Evidence of this is in His elaboration: “that they had been Muslims.” The words “that they had” suggest that their yearning is one of longing, and that they desire Islam in refection upon their past circumstances, which they missed and can never return to. Thus, there is no alternative but Islam as long as they remain in this world.

The verse highlights that those who disbelieve will come to regret their disbelief, wishing they had embraced Islam once the tapestry of this worldly life folds up.

(15:3) Leave them to eat and enjoy and to be diverted by longings.

Soon they will know.

The term ‘diversion’ suggests being sidetracked or consumed. It’s often expressed as: “He was diverted by one thing from another,” implying he was so engrossed in it that he overlooked the latter.

The statement, “Leave them to eat and enjoy and to be diverted,” is a command to let them persist in their falsehood, subtly discouraging any engagement in debates or presenting evidence to them. This suggests that a day will come when they’ll deeply regret not being Muslims, but by then, it will be too late. The phrase “Soon they will know” elucidates the rationale behind this command, emphasizing the futility of arguments and disputes.

Essentially, there’s no need for such confrontations, as they will inevitably recognize the truth in its undeniable clarity.

The verse subtly conveys to them that their primary pursuits in life are merely eating and indulging in worldly pleasures, coupled with being distracted by feeting hopes and dreams. Their rationale aligns more with beasts and other speechless creatures. Given this, it’s only ftting to distance oneself from them and their views, refraining from presenting them with profound arguments rooted in sound intellect and human reasoning.

(15:4-5) We did not destroy any town but that it had a known term. No nation can advance its time nor can it defer it.

These (two) verses serve to afrm and emphasize the preceding verse where it states, “Soon they will know.” According to the context and underlying meaning, this signals that people will not embrace Islam in this

worldly life. Rather, they will desire to convert only after their appointed time has passed and their doom has occurred. In this regard, individuals have no free will; instead, every community has a known book (of record)

with God, detailing their predetermined lifespan. Neither can they hasten it nor delay it by a single moment.

Furthermore, these verses imply that each nation, like each individual, has a designated record. As God states: W e have attached every person’s omen to his neck, and We shall bring it out for him on the Day of

Resurrection as a book that he will fnd wide open (al-Isrā’:13).

(15:6) They said, ‘O you, to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are indeed crazy.’

Their words deviate from the tone of mockery.1 Hence, they addressed the Prophet not by his name but by the characteristic of receiving the Reminder, in line with his claim. Their use of the passive voice highlights their ignorance of the origin of this revelation and refects their lack of faith and trust in the Prophet’s assertion that it is God who revealed it.

The description “to whom the Reminder has been sent down,” and the term “Reminder,” are both intended to mock, just as their statement “you are indeed crazy” aims to discredit and falsify his claims.

1 Editor’s note: In other words, this choice of words could indicate a certain level of hesitancy or uncertainty on their part about the source of the revelation, thus giving the speech a tone that doesn’t entirely align with a straightforward attempt to mock or belittle the Prophet.

(15:7) ‘Why do you not bring us the angels should you be truthful?!’

This employs a form of provocation. The usage of “why do you not”

(law mā) here can be likened to saying “why wouldn’t you,” (hallā) serving to stimulate or challenge the listener. Essentially, it asks, “If your claim of prophethood is genuine, then why not summon the angels as witnesses to validate your message?” This line of questioning closely parallels another verse, “Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he may be a warner with him” (al-Furqan:7).

The rationale behind their demand for angels stems from their perception of humanity as purely material, mired in the vices of lust and anger.

They can’t conceive a link between the human world and the celestial realm of pure light and purity. Therefore, they argue that anyone claiming a connection to that spiritual world must bring forth its inhabitants,

namely the noble angels, to corroborate his claims and support his mission.

However, it’s important to note that in the belief system of the idolaters, angels serve as deities subordinate to God. Thus, their call for monotheism indirectly argues that these lesser gods have no role in intercession or worship, except by God’s decree. If this is true, as they seem to

acknowledge, then the angels should descend to validate and support the prophetic claim.1

(15:8) We do not send down the angels except with due reason, and then they will not be granted any respite.

This serves as a reply to those who suggested to the Prophet that he produce angels as proof of his truthfulness. The core message here is that

1 Editor’s note: When these idolaters call for proof in the form of angels, they are inadvertently invoking their own system of belief where angels have a specifc status as lesser gods. The implication here is somewhat paradoxical: By demanding angels as proof, they are also implicitly accepting the framework of monotheism—that there is a greater deity (Allah) who has control over these lesser gods (the angels).

the Divine Will operates in such a way that His angels remain hidden from human view, shrouded in the realm of the Unseen. Were these angels to be revealed upon their request, it would constitute an extraordinary, celestial sign, breaking the usual norms, descending due to their own proposition.

Following the appearance of such a miraculous sign, prompted by human demand, Divine punishment—eradication and utter ruin—would inevitably ensue if they fail to believe. Given that these staunch disbelievers are

unlikely to embrace faith, their doom would be sealed.

In summary, if God were to send down angels under these circumstances— where people are requesting a decisive, irrefutable sign to manifest

the truth— He would dispatch them with an unequivocal truth that leaves no room for doubt. Following this, they would not be given any more time;

rather, their destruction would be immediate and complete. This captures the essence of what some (commentators) have discussed on the subject.

Another view suggests that “with the truth” in the verse refers to death.

The implication is that angels descend only in association with the inescapable truth that is death, and thereafter, there would be no delay. This

seems to echo God’s words, “The day when they see the angels, there will be no good news for the guilty that day” (al-Furqān:22).

It is also said that “with the truth” signifes the Divine message. That is, angels are dispatched solely for the purpose of revelation and prophetic communication. This appears to align with verses like “The M essenger has certainly brought you the truth” (al-Nisa’:170), and “They have certainly denied the truth when it came to them” (al-An’ām:5).

Various perspectives are discussed in the exegesis of the verse, alongside others that appear in diferent explanations. While each provides some insight, it’s important to note that none of them fts neatly into the constraint implied by the phrase, “We do not send down the angels except with

due reason.” The descent of the angels is not limited solely to the enactment of Divine punishment or eradication, nor is it confned merely to the

realm of death, or solely to delivering revelations and messages. Assigning one of the three aforementioned interpretations to “with due reason” (or, with the truth) would necessitate imposing various limitations, which are efectively negated by the broader, more inclusive tone of the verse itself, as is evident to anyone who reviews the accepted interpretations.

It’s possible to interpret the meaning of the verse through contemplation of other verses, suggesting that our material existence— our life in this world—is a complex interplay of truth and falsehood. Truth doesn’t manifest in its fullness, with all its attributes and consequences, as underscored by the Qur’anic phrase, “This is how Allah compares the truth and falsehood” (al-Ra’d:17). This has been discussed in detail before. In such an environment, any manifestation of truth is also prone to elements of ambiguity and doubt, which is corroborated by our life experiences.

Another supporting point is the Qur’anic verse, “Had We made him an angel, We would have surely made him a man, and We would have surely confounded them just as they confound (the truth now)” (al-An’ām:9).

Life serves as a trial and a realm of choices; these choices exist precisely because of the potential for blurring the lines between truth and falsehood, and between good and evil. This sets the stage for humans to fnd

themselves at the crossroads of divergent paths, discerning good from evil through their respective indicators (or signs) and outcomes, and then making a choice that leads to either happiness or misery.

Concerning the realm of angels and their existential state, it is a realm of pure truth, untainted by any falsehood. This is evidenced by the Qur’anic verses: “Over which are (assigned) angels, severe and mighty, who do not disobey whatever Allah has commanded them, and carry out what they are commanded” (al-Taḥrīm:6) and “Rather they are (His) honored servants.

They do not venture to speak ahead of Him, and they act by His command”

(al-Anbiyā’:26-27).

The verses imply that the angels are distinguished beings: noble and radiant, untainted by defciencies or imperfections. They stand beyond the realm of evil, misery, corruption, and disobedience. Hence, the material framework, built upon choices, probabilities, and the spectrum of right and wrong, obedience and defance, joy and sorrow, is not applicable to them. A more comprehensive discussion on this subject will follow, God w illing.

In the subsequent discussions, it will be highlighted that as long as humans are submerged in the material world and its allurements, similar to the disbelievers and those astray, they cannot attain the realm of pure truth. The sole pathway to this understanding is by transitioning from their current state to the realm of absolute truth, where obscurities are unveiled as indicated by the verse: You were certainly oblivious of this. W e have removed your veil from you, and so your sight is acute today” (Qaf:22).

In the human perspective, this realm is identifed as the Hereafter.1 The appearance of the angelic realm to humans immersed in the material world is contingent on a change in circumstance— essentially, the transition from this life to the afterlife, which is death. However, exceptions

exist among God’s chosen servants and purifed allies who are free from the stains of sin and are close to His divine presence. These individuals possess the ability to perceive the unseen even while existing in the physical world, like the Prophets (peace be upon them).

Perhaps what we’re highlighting aligns with “We do not send down the angels except with due reason, and then they will not be granted any respite.”

The plea for the angels to descend was a desire to witness them in their true forms as a testament to belief. However, such a vision is only possible after death as God stated: “Those who do not expect to encounter Us say, ‘Why have angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?’

Certainly they are full of arrogance within their souls and have become terribly defant. The day when they see the angels, there will be no good news for

the guilty that day, and they will say, ‘Keep away (from paradise)!’ Then we shall attend to the works they have done and then turn them into scattered dust” (al-Furqān:21-23).

This dual meaning is also present in the verse: “Had We made him an angel, We would have surely made him a man, and We would have surely confounded them just as they confound (the truth now)” (al-’An`ām:9).

This means that if angels were sent down as miraculous signs confrming prophethood, it would necessitate divine judgment upon the people.

Similarly, if an angel were assigned prophethood, he would have to be portrayed as a human being, capable of being misunderstood or doubted.

This is because divine testing and tribulation require the possibility of both success and failure, salvation and doom.

1 Editor’s note: Being “engrossed in this material world” implies a focus on worldly desires and distractions that can cloud spiritual insight. The verse quoted by the author from Sūrah Qafihighlights the moment these veils lift, granting clear vision in the Hereafter, emphasizing the feeting nature of worldly life against the eternal reality beyond.

(15:9) Indeed We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will preserve it.

This verse emphasizes exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ), particularly in response to those who rejected the Qur’an, describing it as mere delusions or denouncing the Prophet as mad. They implied that his message and creation were meaningless. By demanding the descent of angels, they sought validation of the Prophets call about Qur’an’s authenticity and its status as a true heavenly book.

The meaning—and God knows best—is that this Reminder wasn’t brought by the Prophet from his own accord. Thus, adversaries cannot undermine or counteract it with obstinacy. The Prophet isn’t burdened with its preservation, nor does it stem from angels requiring their afrmation. Instead, We have gradually revealed this Reminder, overseeing its

preservation given its inherent nature as a Reminder coupled with Our profound protection.

The Reminder (that is, the Qur’an) is living and eternal, safeguarded from death and oblivion from its origin. It’s shielded from any additions that would compromise its essence as a Reminder, likewise from any reductions. It’s also preserved from any alterations in its form and arrangement

that would change its characteristic as a divine Reminder, elucidating the realities of His wisdom.

The verse indicates that God’s Book is safeguarded from any alterations in its entirety, as it serves as a divine Reminder. Consequently, it stands as a living and enduring Reminder.

A comparable verse indicating that the revered Book is divinely protected, free from any tampering or changes, being a Reminder from God,

states: “Indeed those who defy the Reminder when it comes to them. Indeed it is an august Book: falsehood cannot approach it, from before it nor from behind it, (gradually) sent down (revelation) from One all-wise, all-laudable” (Fussilat:41-42). From prior discussions, it becomes evident that the particles “alif” and “lam” in the “Reminder” (al-dhikr) pertains to the covenant of remembrance. The term “guardians” in this context denotes a sense of reception,

as inferred from the active participle form. This clarifcation addresses potential claims suggesting that if the verse implied the Qur’an’s immunity to distortion due to its status as a Reminder, the same would apply to

the Torah and the Gospel, given that they too are regarded as Reminders.

However, the divine discourse clearly acknowledges the presence of distortions in both these texts.1

W ith the context of the verse in focus, it underscores the eternal preservation of the Reminder, which refers to the Qur’an, post its divine revelation. The verse doesn’t suggest any elevated status of the Reminder in

terms of divine protection but keeps the emphasis squarely on its content and signifcance.

Further insights on this matter will be explored, God willing.

Examining Narrations

(1) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, with his chain of narration from his father, from Ibn Abī ‘Umayr, from ‘Umar b. Udhayna, from Rafā‘a, from Imām al-Ṣādiq who said: “On the Day of Resurrection, a caller will announce from the side of God: ‘None shall enter Paradise except a Muslim.’ On that day, those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims. He then recited: “Leave them to eat and enjoy and to be diverted by longings (by their activities). Soon they will know” (15:3).

Author’s Comment: A similar narration about the commentary of this verse has been reported by al-ʿAyyāshī, on the authority of ʿAṭāʾ al-M akkī, from both Imām al-Bāqir and Imām al-Ṣādiq.

(2) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Ibn Mardawayh with a sound chain of narration reported from Jābir b.

‘Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of God stated: “There will be people from my community who will be punished for their sins, and they will remain in Hellfre as long as God wills. The polytheists will mock them, saying, ‘We do not see any beneft from

your belief.’ No believer will remain except that God Almighty will eventually remove him from the Hellfre. The Messenger of God then recited: “M uch will the faithless wish that they had been M uslim s.”

1 Editor’s note: While all three texts—the Qur’an, the Torah, and the Gospel—are divine Reminders, only the Qur’an is highlighted for its unique preservation, emphasizing its distinct status amidst recognized distortions in both the other scriptures.

Author’s Comment: This same meaning has been reported in various ways on the authority of Abū Mūsā al-Ashaʿrī, Abū Saʿīd al-Khuḍrī, and Anas b. Mālik from the Messenger of God.

(3) In al-Durr al-manthūr, on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn al-Shāhīn’s Sharḥ madhāhib ahl al-sunnah, on the authority of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib who said: The Messenger of God said: “Indeed, those who commit major sins from the monotheists of all nations, who die upon their major sins without remorse or repentance, if they enter Hellfre, their eyes will not turn blue, their faces will not turn black, they will not be chained with the devils, they won’t be shackled with chains, they won’t drink boiling water, and they won’t wear pitch. God has forbidden their bodies from eternal damnation due to monotheism and protected them from the fre because of their prostration. Among them, some will have the fre reaching their feet, some to their heels, some to their thighs, some to their waists, and some to their necks, depending on their sins and deeds. Some will remain in it for a month and then be taken out, some for a year and then be taken out, and the longest stay will be equivalent to the duration of the worldly life from the day it was created to the day it ends. When God wishes to remove them from it, the Jews, Christians, and others in Hellfre from other religions will say to the monotheists in Hellfre: ‘You believed in God, His Books, and His Messengers, yet today we and you are the same in the fre.’ At that point, God’s displeasure with them will be unparalleled, and He will move them from the fre to a spring between Heaven and the Path. They will grow there like the plants that grow rapidly in a torrent’s residue. Afterward, they will enter Paradise with an inscription on their foreheads: ‘These are the inmates of Hell, freed by the M erciful.’ They will reside in Paradise as long as God wills. Then, they will ask God Almighty to erase that inscription from their foreheads. God will send an angel to erase it. Then God will send angels with nails of fre who will seal those who remain in Hell with those nails. God will then forget them beside His Throne, and the inhabitants of Paradise will be preoccupied with their bounties and pleasures. This is what is meant by the verse: Much will the faithless wish that they had been Muslims.

Author’s Comment: al-Tarthūth is a plant, and ḥamīl al-sayl refers to its residue carried by the torrent. Narrations from the Shiite sources have been reported that are close in meaning to this tradition.

(4) In al-Durr al-manthūr, Ahmad and Ibn Mardawaih narrate from Abū Saʿīd al-Khuḍrī that the Messenger of God planted a stick in front of him, another beside him, and another behind him. He asked, “Do you know what this is?” They replied, “God and His Messenger know best.” He said, “This stick represents the human, the one beside him signifes his lifespan, and the one behind him represents his hopes. M an pursues his hopes, but his lifespan interrupts it before he realizes.” I say: A narration with a similar meaning has also been conveyed through diferent chains from Anas.

Author’s Comment: A similar narration has also been reported on the authority of Anas from the Messenger of God.

(5) In M ajma’ al-bayyān al-bayān, from Amīr al-Muʾminīn, he said, “The two things I fear most for you are following desires and long hopes, for following desires prevents you from the truth, and long hopes make you forget the Hereafter.”

(6) And in Tafsīr al-Qummī, regarding His saying, “We do not send down the angels except in truth, and they would not be given any respite” he said, “If we were to send down the angels, they would not be given any respite and they would be destroyed.”

An Excursus on the Qur’an being Immune to Distortion (In Seven Sections)

Section One

Approximately fourteen centuries ago, the Arabian Prophet named Muḥammad declared his prophethood and embarked on his mission. This invitation was accepted by a group comprising both Arabs and non-Arabs.

He presented a book, attributed to his Lord, which he named the Qur’an.

This book articulated various teachings and the foundational tenets of the Divine Law to which he called people. He used the Qur’an as a testament to his mission, referring to it as a sign of his prophethood. It’s an established historical truth that the Qur’an in our possession today is the very same one the Prophet brought forth and recited to his contemporaries. This implies that the text of the Qur’an has remained unaltered; it was never replaced by another, be it in a similar or diferent style, and then later circulated as the original Qur’an revealed to the Prophet. Only someone with impaired understanding could doubt this veracity. All scholars who have researched the topic of the distortion of the Qur’an, regardless of their stance, haven’t considered such a drastic alteration.

The only variations these scholars have contemplated involve minor adjustments— perhaps an added or omitted sentence or verse, or slight changes in wording or diacritics. Nevertheless, they unanimously agree that the core of the Qur’an has been preserved since the Prophet’s time, with nothing added or omitted.

Furthermore, the Qur’an showcases distinct qualities across all its verses. The version we have today embodies the attributes it professes to possess, and none of these characteristics have been modifed or lost. The Qur’an also challenges humanity with its eloquence. The style exhibited in our current version is exceptionally magnifcent. This unparalleled style surpasses all known speeches from the most eloquent Arabs, whether in poetry, prose, speeches, letters, dialogues, or other forms. Such a style is consistently present throughout its verses.

The Qur’an also poses a challenge, asserting its consistency through the verse: “Do they not contemplate the Qur’an? Had it been from (someone) other than Allah, they would have surely found much discrepancy in it”

(al-Nisa’:82). That which we have received perfectly embodies this claim.

Should there be any ambiguity or perceived faw in a verse, another verse will elucidate it. In essence, what might seem a,s inconsistencies or contradictions at an initial glance are expounded upon elsewhere in the book.

The Qur’an presents various challenges, some of which are comprehensible even to those who are not fuent in Arabic. For instance, it declares:

“Say, ‘Should all humans and jinn rally to bring the like of this Qur’an, they will not bring the like of it, even if they assisted one another’” (al-Isrā’:88).

And again: “It is indeed a decisive word, and it is not a jest” (al-Ṭāriq:13-14).

The rendition of the Qur’an we have today lucidly conveys the truth, leaving no space for doubt. It guides us to the pinnacle of understanding—

be it the fundamentals of genuine knowledge, the overarching tenets of natural law, or the nuances of moral virtue. In its teachings, we fnd no inadequacies, contradictions, or errors. Every tenet aligns with the unifying spirit of monotheism, which serves as the foundational principle all

Qur’anic teachings return to, whether examined individually or collectively.

Furthermore, the Qur’an is rich with narratives of past prophets and their communities. The version available to us today narrates these accounts in a manner that aligns with pure faith, emphasizing the revered status of prophethood and the prophets’ unwavering devotion. When juxtaposing the Qur’anic tales of prophets with their counterparts in the Old

and New Testament, it becomes evident that the Qur’an portrays them in the most dignifed manner.

The Qur’an contains numerous verses that speak of future battles and events. The version of the Qur’an we have today confrms these prophecies.

The Qur’an also describes itself with various admirable attributes. It is referred to as a light and a guide leading to the straight path and fostering a righteous community. Indeed, the version we have in our hands today embodies all these characteristics, ofering comprehensive guidance.

One of the most signifcant attributes that the Qur’an ascribes to itself is being a “reminder of God.” It serves as God’s perpetual and living sign.

Through its verses, it elucidates His beautiful names, His sublime attributes, the method of His creation, His angels, His scriptures, His messengers, and His decrees. The Qur’an details the culmination of creation,

including the resurrection and everything’s return to God. It discusses the eventual outcomes of souls, whether in success or despair, and elaborates on the intricacies of heaven and hell. All these elements remind us

of God, mirroring how the Qur’an serves as a reminder with its defnitive truths. The version we possess today encompasses all these facets of being a divine reminder.

“Remembrance” (dhikr) is one of the most encompassing descriptions of the Qur’an’s role. Hence, it’s referred to as the Reminder in verses

highlighting its protection from falsehood, alteration, and distortion. For instance, the verse states, “Indeed those who commit sacrilege in Our signs are not hidden from Us. Is someone who is cast in the Fire better of, or someone who arrives safely on the Day of Resurrection? Act as you wish; indeed He sees best what you do. Indeed those who defy the Reminder when it comes to them. Indeed it is an august Book: falsehood cannot approach it, from before it nor from behind it, (gradually) sent down (revelation) from One all-wise, all-laudable” (Fussilat:40-42). This emphasizes that falsehood cannot infltrate the Qur’an, be it through refutation, replacement, alteration, or distortion. Any of these would invalidate its attribute as a reminder.

The Qur’an is also termed the Reminder in another verse discussing its preservation: “Indeed We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will preserve it” (15:9). This asserts that God has safeguarded the Qur’an from any change, be it in wording or sequence, ensuring it always serves as a reminder of Him.

Some have mistakenly assumed that the pronoun “it” in the previously mentioned verse refers to the Prophet. However, this interpretation

lacks a solid foundation. The context of the verse itself contradicts such a viewpoint. The disbelievers ridiculed the Prophet primarily due to the Qur’an, which he asserted was revealed to him by God. This sentiment is echoed in a verse we’ve previously discussed: “They said, ‘O you, to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are indeed crazy’” (15:6).

From what we’ve detailed, it’s clear that the Qur’an, which God revealed to His Prophet, and described as a preserved dhikr (reminder), remains intact. It is divinely shielded against any additions, subtractions, or alterations, just as God promised His Prophet.

In conclusion, the Qur’an was sent down by God to His Prophet and is characterized in many verses with specifc qualities. If any of these characteristics were altered— whether through addition, subtraction, or a change in wording or sequence—it would undoubtedly afect that particular attribute. However, the Qur’an we have with us fully embodies

these described attributes in the best possible way. There has been no distortion that deprives it of any of its qualities. The Qur’an we possess is the very one revealed to the Prophet. If we assume a verse was omitted or a change in grammar, letter, or sequence occurred, it must be in a manner that does not afect any of its qualities, such as its inimitability, superiority over other divine scriptures, guidance, luminosity, and its nature as a dhikr (reminder). This could be, for example, a repetitive verse being omitted or a minor diference in a dot or infection, and the like.

Section Two

There are many narrations from the Prophet, transmitted through both Shīʿah and Sunnī channels, that instruct us to refer to the Qur’an during times of confusion and to resolve dilemmas. These narrations afrm the absence of any distortion in the Qur’an.

Furthermore, the frequently cited “Hadith of the two weighty things”

Section Six

The narrations discussed in the two preceding sections are among the most renowned concerning the compilation of the Qur’an. They vary between authentic and inauthentic. These reports suggest that the initial ofcial compilation of the Qur’an during Abū Bakr’s reign involved compiling various sūrahs (chapters) that had been inscribed on palm stalks, thin

white stones, shoulder blades, animal hides, and pieces of leather. Dispersed verses were appropriately integrated into their corresponding sūrahs.

The second ofcial compilation during ʿUthmān’s reign aimed to align the widespread versions of the Qur’an with the ofcial version from the frst compilation. This efort emerged due to discrepancies appearing in individual copies and the existence of variant readings. The goal was to consolidate the recitations into one uniformed copy. A noteworthy distinction between the second and the initial compilation is that Zayd incorporated the verse: “Among the faithful are men who have been true to their covenant with Allah...” (al-Aḥzāb: 23) into Sūrah al-Aḥzāb. Before this incorporation, this verse was absent from the Qur’an for ffteen years.

Furthermore, al-Bukhārī narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr who said: I asked ʿUthmān, regarding the verse, “Those of you who die and leave widows”

which another verse had abrogated, “Why did you neither keep it nor omit it?” ʿUthmān replied, “Oh nephew, I won’t change any of it from its place.”

Anyone who examines these narrations impartially will observe that, while they are singular and not frequently narrated (not tawātur), they are supported by unassailable external evidences. The Prophet communicated every revelation he received. He withheld nothing, educating and elucidating for his followers the meanings of what was divinely sent down to

him— a fact explicitly stated in the Qur’an. Following his passing, a segment of his community persistently devoted themselves to the study and teaching of the Qur’an—both its meanings and recitation. They were known as

the “Reciters of the Qur’an” (qurrāʾ). Regrettably, many of them perished in the Battle of Yamāmah.

Despite this loss, the fervor to learn and recite the Qur’an remained undiminished among the people. The Qur’an was never absent from the Muslim community, not even for a fraction of a day, until it was consolidated into a singular manuscript upon which consensus was reached. Thus,

the Qur’an was preserved from the alterations that befell the Torah, the Gospel, and scriptures of other prophets.

Additionally, there exists an abundance of narrations in both Shīʿah and Sunnī traditions that describe the Prophet frequently reciting numerous Qur’anic chapters in the obligatory daily prayers and other recommended prayers. These recitations were heard publicly. The majority of

the Qur’anic chapters, whether revealed in M ecca or M edina, are named in these traditions.

Furthermore, the narration from ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ regarding the verse: “Indeed, Allah enjoins justice and kindness...” (al-Naḥl:90)

highlights that the Prophet remarked, “Gabriel brought this verse to me and instructed me to position it correctly within the chapter.” Similar narrations suggest the Prophet recited entire chapters of the Qur’an, like Āl

ʿImrān, al-Nisāʾ, among others. This implies that he directed the scribes of revelation to appropriately position certain verses within their respective chapters. Having elaborated on this, we emphasize that the most compelling evidence that the Qur’an remains unchanged is what we mentioned at the outset of this discourse. The Qur’an in our hands today possesses all the honorable attributes described by God Himself.

To summarize the essence of the narrations we’ve discussed:

Firstly: The text we have between the covers, referred to as the Qur’an, is undoubtedly the Word of God. It has neither seen additions nor undergone any alterations. However, while nothing has been changed or added,

we cannot decisively deny the potential omission of certain parts. For instance, there are multiple reports suggesting that ʿUmar frequently referred to the so-called “verse of stoning.” Yet, this verse didn’t make its way into the ofcial text that we have now. The numerous narrations regarding this—which, according to Ālūsī in his Tafsīr, are too many to enumerate— do not suggest that these verses were annulled in recitation.

We’ve already established the inaccuracy of such a claim. Asserting that some verses were annulled in recitation from the Qur’an and thus omitted is even more controversial than the assertion of distortion.

Furthermore, those who owned personal copies of the Qur’an, like ʿAlī, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, did not contest the content of the ofcial version. An exception to this is the account that Ibn

Masʿūd did not include Sūrah al-Falaq and Sūrah al-Nās in his personal manuscript. He believed: “These two chapters are a remedy sent down by Gabriel to the M essenger of God specifcally for al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn.”

However, this view was contested by other companions and the Imāms.

Reports confrming them as chapters of the Qur’an are overwhelmingly numerous (tawātur).

In essence, while these narrations are individual accounts, they are corroborated by strong contextual evidence. They convincingly negate any

additions or alterations to the Qur’an. However, they don’t conclusively dismiss the idea of omissions. They merely challenge this on a speculative level. Some argue that the reports on the Qur’an being modifed through addition, change, or omission are widespread (tawātur), but these claims are unfounded.

The primary reason for our argument is the evidence we put forth at the start of our research. The Qur’an that is present with us today possesses the illustrious qualities with which God has described the genuine

Qur’an He revealed to His M essenger. These qualities encompass it being a clear statement, an eliminator of disputes, a reminder, a guide, a light, a clarifer of authentic knowledge and natural laws, and a miraculous sign, among its other noble attributes.

Building on this point, it’s imperative to understand that the Qur’an’s claim to being the Word of God revealed to His Messenger is supported by these very eminent qualities. It does not require any external afrmation.

This means that the Qur’an doesn’t depend on widespread transmission or nearly widespread transmission as long as these attributes are inherent within it. On the contrary, the Qur’an, characterized by these grand

qualities, is evidence of its trustworthiness. This sets it apart from other books and scripts attributed to their respective authors. Likewise, it’s distinct from scholars’ statements, which rely on defnitive transmission and

extensive or near-extensive reporting for validation. The Qur’an’s proof of authenticity is intrinsic.

In summary, the aforementioned narrations, as you can see, are individual ones surrounded by defnitive indicators negating any tampering,

be it through additions or alterations, with absolute certainty except for assumptions. The claim of some regarding continuous transmission from three perspectives lacks a solid foundation.

To rely on this perspective is based on the argument we introduced at the beginning of these investigations: that the Qur’an in our possession embodies those noble attributes by which God has described the real Qur’an that He revealed to His M essenger. This signifes that the evidence of the Qur’an, in proving that it is the Speech of God sent down to His M essenger, is its very self, adorned with those distinguished attributes. This understanding does not hinge on any external factor; its evidence stands frm wherever it is established, in the hands of whoever it may be, and by whatever means it reaches us.

In other words, the Qur’an, which descended from God to the Prophet, does not rely on its noble attributes based on its confrmed transmission to him through continuous or frequent transmission, even if it possesses that.

Instead, the matter is the opposite. Its possession of these noble attributes is the proof for its transmission. This is unlike books and letters attributed to authors and writers, or the sayings reported from scholars and thinkers, which require defnite transmission, or at least frequent or abundant

transmission, to be considered authentic. The very essence of the Qur’an is the evidence for its authenticity.

Secondly: The arrangement of the chapters (sūrahs) comes from the companions during the frst and second compilations. Evidence for this is what has been previously mentioned in the traditions regarding ‘Uthman’s placement of al-Anfāl and al-Barāʾah between al-A’rāfiand Yūnus, even though they were positioned later in the frst compilation.

Another piece of evidence is the variations in the order of the chapters in the Qur’an of other companions compared to the frst and second

compilations. It has been reported that the Qur’an of ʿAlī was arranged according to the order of revelation. It began with al-ʿAlaq, followed by al-M uddaththir, then al-Qalam, then al-M uzzammil, then al-M asad, then al-Takwīr, and so on until the end of the Meccan and Medinan revelations.

This order was mentioned in al-Itqan as reported from Ibn Fāris. In Tārikh al-Yaʿqūbī, another order for ʿAlī’s Qur’an is mentioned.

It is reported from Ibn Ashṭah in his Kitāb al-M aṣāḥifs that, based on his chain of narrators from Abū Ja’far al-Kūfī, the arrangement of Abū (someone’s) codex signifcantly deviates from the commonly accepted version of the Qur’an. Similarly, through his narration from Jarīr b. ‘Abdul

Ḥamīd, he describes the arrangement of ‘Abdullāh b. Mas’ūd’s codex. This arrangement starts with the longer chapters, followed by those roughly a hundred verses in length, then the medium length chapters, and fnally the short chapters. This order also contrasts with the widely accepted version of the Qur’an. Many scholars hold the view that the arrangement of the chapters in the Qur’an is divinely ordained, asserting that the Prophet Muhammad was commanded to arrange them in this order through guidance from the Angel Gabriel, by the command of God Almighty. Some even went to the extreme of claiming that this has been transmitted through continuous chains of narrators. One wonders where this continuous chain is, given that the main narrations on this subject have already been presented, and they contain no such indication. There will also be a discussion on some scholars’ evidence for this claim, which is based on the belief that the Qur’an was frst sent down in its entirety to the lowest heaven from the Preserved Tablet, and then revealed in stages to the Prophet M uhammad.

Thirdly: The placement of certain Qur’anic verses, which were revealed separately and are now located where they are, was not devoid of intervention by the companions through their independent reasoning. This is

evident from the narrations regarding the frst compilation, as previously mentioned.

As for the narration from ‘Uthmān b. Abī al-’Ās from the Prophet which states, “Gabriel came to me and instructed me to place this verse in this particular position of the chapter: ‘Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct’ (the verse),” it does not necessarily indicate that the Prophet did this for every verse. If we were to assume this narration as reliable, it still does not provide evidence when we consider the preceding narrations that the Companions’ arrangement aligned with that of the Prophet. Mere positive assumptions about the Companions do not allow for narrations to serve as evidence of this. What it does suggest is that they would not intentionally deviate from the order he had conveyed for verses they were familiar with, but not necessarily for those they were unaware of.

In the earlier narrations regarding the frst compilation, it becomes evident that they were not fully aware of the positions of all the verses, nor the essence of them.

This understanding is further supported by extensive narrations from both Shi’a and Sunni sources which indicate that the Prophet and the believers would only come to know the completion of a chapter when the Basmala (Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm) was revealed. This is narrated by Abū Dāwūd, al-Hākim, al-Bayhaqī, and al-Bazzār via Sa’īd b. Jubayr as found in al-Itqān, quoting Ibn ‘Abbās saying, “The Prophet would not recognize the conclusion of a chapter until ‘In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the M ost M erciful’ was revealed to him.” al-Bazzār added, “W hen it was revealed, he recognized that the chapter had ended, and another one began or was facing him.”

was revealed. Once it was revealed, they knew that the chapter had concluded.” Its chain of narration meets the criteria of both al-Bukhāri and

Muslim.

Further, from al-Hākim through another source from Sa’īd, quoting Ibn ‘Abbās: “Whenever Gabriel came to the Prophet and recited ‘In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful’, he knew it introduced a new chapter.” The chain of this narration is authentic.

Comment: Similar narrations to this have been conveyed in several other reports, and this has also been narrated through Shi’a sources from al-Bāqir.

The narrations, as you see, are explicit in their indication that verses were arranged by the Prophet according to the order of revelation. Thus, verses revealed in M ecca were in M akki chapters, and those revealed in M adīnah were in M adanī chapters, unless a chapter was revealed partly in Mecca and partly in Madīnah. This exception only applies to a single chapter.

This necessitates the view that the observed diferences in the placements of verses are based on the independent reasoning (ijtihād) of the

companions.

To clarify, there are countless narrations regarding the reasons for revelation, which indicate that many verses in M adanī chapters were revealed

in M ecca, and vice versa. Also, some verses of the Qur’an, revealed towards the end of the Prophet’s era, are found in chapters that were revealed at the beginning of the Hijrah. Between these times, many other chapters were revealed. An example is Sūrah al-Baqarah, which was revealed in the frst year of the Hijrah. It contains the verses about usury (ribā), and the narrations suggest they are among the last verses to be revealed to the Prophet. It

has been narrated that ‘Umar b. al-Khaṭṭāb said, “The Messenger of God passed away without explaining the verses of usury to us.” Among these verses is the saying of God: “And fear a Day when you will be returned to God” (al-Baqarah:281). It has been reported that this was the last verse revealed to the Prophet.

These verses, which are scattered in topic and are placed in chapters that don’t align with their Makki or Madanī classifcation, are positioned out of their chronological order of revelation, and this seems to be due to the independent reasoning of the companions.

Supporting this is what is mentioned in al-Itqān from Ibn Ḥajar al-‘Asqalānī, where it has been narrated that ‘Alī b. Abī Ṭālib collected the Qur’an in the order of revelation shortly after the death of the Prophet.

This narration is documented by Ibn Abī Dāwūd and stands as one of the consistent evidences in the narrations of the Shi’a.

This is what is indicated by the apparent narrations of the aforementioned section. However, the majority insist that the ordering of the verses

is divinely prescribed. The verses of the M uṣḥafithat circulates today, which is the Uthmānī Muṣḥaf, are arranged as the Prophet ordered, under the guidance of Gabriel. They interpret the apparent narrations to mean that the companions’ compilation was not about ordering but rather was a collection of what they knew and memorized from the Prophet concerning the chapters and their arranged verses, bound together in one place.

You are well-aware that the nature of the initial compilation, as indicated by the narrations, categorically refutes this claim.

Some might use as evidence what some have claimed as a consensus on this matter. al-Suyūṭī relayed in al-Itqān from al-Zarkashī the claim of a consensus on this, and from Abū Ja’far b. al-Zubayr, there’s a negation of any diference in this matter among Muslims. This is a reported consensus that should not be relied upon, especially after the existence of disagreement on the original alteration and the implications of the aforementioned

narrations against it.

And sometimes they provide evidence based on the concept of tawātur (continuous, corroborated narration). This is found in the statements of many of them who claimed the continuity of the present order from the Prophet. This claim is astounding. It is conveyed in al-Itqān after quoting what was narrated by al-Bukhārī and others through various chains

from Anas, who said: “The Prophet passed away, and the Qur’ān was not compiled by anyone except four: Abū al-Dardā’, Mu’ādh b. Jabal, Zayd b. Thābit, and Abū Zayd.” In another narration, it says “ʿUbayy b. Ka’b”

instead of Abū al-Dardā’. al-M āzarī stated regarding this: “A group of heretics clung to this statement of Anas, but we do not concede to their interpretation of it. We admit it in its apparent sense, but how can they claim

that the actual matter is as such? We admit it, but it does not necessarily mean that if many did not memorize the entire Qur’ān, then the majority didn’t memorize its compilation. It is not a condition for tawātur that every individual must memorize the entirety; rather, if everyone memorizes the whole, even if distributed among them, it sufces.”

As for his claim that the apparent meaning of Anas’s statement is not intended, this is something that should not be heeded in linguistic research based on the apparent wording unless supported by evidence from the speaker’s statement or a suitable alternative. M erely making a claim or relying on another’s statement does not sufce.

Certainly, if Anas’s words were interpreted contrary to their apparent meaning, it would have been necessary to understand that these four

only compiled, during the Prophet’s time, the majority of the Qur’ān and most of its chapters and verses. It’s not that they and other companions compiled the entire Qur’ān as in the M usḥafial-’Uthmānī, memorized the order of its chapters and verses, and knew the position of each verse in relation to the others. Zayd b. Thābit himself—who is one of the four mentioned in Anas’s narration and the one responsible for both the frst and second compilations— explicitly states in his narrations that he did not memorize all the verses.

Similarly, in al-Itqān, from Ibn Ashṭah in al-M uṣḥaf, with an authentic chain, from Muḥammad b. Sīrīn, it was said: “Abū Bakr died without having compiled the Qur’ān, and ‘Umar was killed without having compiled

the Qur’ān.”

As for his statement: “We accept it, but where do they get the idea that the actual matter is as such?” It can be countered with: “Where does this claimant get the idea that the reality is as he claims, especially when the evidences are known to contradict what he claims?”

As for his statement: “It is sufcient for ensuring tawātur (consecutive transmission) that everyone memorizes the entire Qur’ān through distribution,” this is a clear fallacy. Because this only indicates that the entirety of

the Qur’ān, as a whole, is transmitted by tawātur. However, the fact that each and every one of the Qur’ānic verses is memorized in its specifc place and context by tawātur is not evident, and this is clear.

In al-Itqān, it’s transmitted from al-Baghawī who said in his Sharḥ al-Sunnah: “The Companions compiled the Qur’ān between the two covers, which God revealed to His Messenger, without adding or omitting anything from it, fearing some of it might be lost with the departure

of its memorizers. They wrote it as they heard it from the Messenger of God, without advancing or delaying anything, or imposing an order they did not take from the Messenger of God. The Messenger of God used to instruct his companions and teach them what was revealed to him from the Qur’ān in the order that is now in our Muṣḥafs, with Jibrīl dictating that to him and informing him, upon the revelation of every verse, that ‘this verse should be written after such-and-such verse in such-and-such chapter’. It’s confrmed that the efort of the Companions was in compiling it in one place, not in ordering it. Indeed, the Qur’ān is written in the

Lawḥ al-M aḥfūẓ (Preserved Tablet) in this order. God revealed it all at once to the nearest heaven, then He revealed it piecemeal as needed. The order of revelation is diferent from the order of recitation.”

And it was transmitted from Ibn al-Ḥaṣār who said: “The arrangement of the sūrahs and the placement of the verses in their positions was indeed by revelation. The Messenger of God used to say: ‘Place such-and-such verse in such-and-such position.’ Certainty has been attained from the consecutively transmitted reports about this order from the M essenger of God. And the Companions only agreed to place it this way in the Muṣḥaf.

End of quote.” And it was also transmitted, something similar, from a group of others like al-Bayhaqī, al-Ṭaybī, and Ibn Ḥajar.

As for their statement: “The Companions compiled the Qur’ān between the two covers, which God revealed to His Messenger, without adding or omitting anything from it” there is nothing among the preceding narrations that indicates this. W hat is confrmed from their implications is that they only afrmed what was proven by evidence regarding the text of the verses. There’s no indication in that about the manner of arranging the verses that were revealed separately. However, it is clear, yes, in the narration from Ibn ‘Abbās about ‘Uthmān that points to this, but the matter

is that he used to instruct some of the revelation scribes with that, which is diferent from informing all the Companions. And that narration contradicts the reports of the frst compilation and the news of the descent of

Bismillah and others.

And as for their statement: “Indeed, the Prophet taught the Companions this order present in our Maṣāḥifithrough a directive from Gabriel and heavenly revelation,” it seems to be a reference to the hadith of ‘Uthmān b. Abī al-’Āṣ, previously mentioned, regarding the verse “Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct.” As you’ve learned from what has been mentioned, it is a single narration concerning a specifc position of a single verse. And how does that compare to the positions of all the scattered verses?

As for their statement: “the Qur’ān is written in the Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ (Preserved Tablet) in this order. God revealed it all at once to the nearest heaven, then He revealed it piecemeal as needed.”— this is an allusion to what has been extensively reported from both the Shi’a and Sunni channels concerning the Qur’an’s descent all at once from the Preserved Tablet

to the nearest heaven, and then its subsequent piecemeal revelation to the Prophet. However, the narrations do not have the slightest indication that the Qur’an was written in the Preserved Tablet and organized in the nearest heaven in the order found in the Muṣḥaf1 we have, and this is evident.

Certainly, there will be a discussion, if God wills, about the meaning of the Qur’an being written on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Maḥfūẓ)

and its descent to the nearest heaven in the context of the verses that are relevant to this, such as the beginnings of Sūrah al-Zukhrūfiand Sūrah al-Dukhān, and Sūrah al-Qadr.

As for their statement: “Indeed, certainty has been attained through continuous transmission from the Messenger of God regarding this order present in the Maṣāḥif,” you have come to know that it is a claim devoid of evidence. This continuous transmission is not known concerning each verse, and how can it be when numerous narrations mention that Ibn Mas’ūd did not include the chapters of protection (Mu’awwidhatayn) in his M uṣḥaf, stating they were not part of the Qur’ān. Instead, he believed that Gabriel revealed them as protections for Ḥasan and Ḥusayn. He used to exclude them from the M aṣāḥif. No report suggests that he ever retracted this statement. So, how could this continuous transmission have remained hidden from him throughout his life after the initial compilation?

Section Seven

The discussion is related to the previous research regarding the narrations of forgetting. A general reference has been made to them, and they

are several narrations reported through the channels of Ahl al-Sunnah concerning the abrogation and forgetting of the Qur’ān. They attributed to these narrations what has been reported about tampering with the Qur’ān, either through omission or alteration.

Here are examples of these reports:

(1) In al-Durr al-manthūr, from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Hākim regarding honorifc titles, Ibn ‘Adī, and Ibn ‘Asākir, from Ibn ‘Abbās who said:

“What used to be revealed to the Prophet at night, he would forget by day.

So, God revealed: ‘W hatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring forth (in place of it) a better verse or similar.’”

(2) In the same source, from Abū Dāwūd regarding abrogations, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalā’il, from Abū ‘Umāmah: A group from the Anṣār, companions of the Prophet, informed him that a man woke up in the middle of the night intending to recite a chapter he had committed to memory,

yet he couldn’t remember anything from it except “Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm.” This happened to some of his companions. They inquired from the Messenger of God about the chapter. He remained silent for a moment and didn’t respond. Then he said: “It was abrogated last night, and it was removed from their chests and from everywhere it was present.”

Comment: The story is narrated through several channels, in terms that are closely related in content.

(3) In the same source, from ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd b. Manṣūr, Abū Dāwūd in his book on abrogation, his son in al-Maṣāḥif, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-M undhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Hākim, who authenticated it from Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ: He read, “W hatever verse We abrogate or cause to be postponed...” It was said to him: “Indeed, Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib reads it as ‘cause to be forgotten.’” Saʿd responded, “The Qur’ān was not revealed to al-Musayyib nor to the family of al-Musayyib. God said: ‘We shall make you recite (the Qur’ān) so you shall not forget it,’ and ‘Remember your Lord when you forget.’”

Comment: By holding onto the two verses, he means that God removed forgetfulness from the Prophet, so it is necessary to read it as “cause to be postponed” from al-nasī’, meaning to leave or delay. Thus, by saying “W hatever verse We abrogate...” it means removing the verse from practice without removing it from recitation, like the verse of ṣadaqah al-najwā. And by saying “or cause to be postponed,” it means leaving the verse and lifting it from them entirely, removing it from both practice and recitation, as its interpretation has been narrated in this manner from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others.

4) In the same source, Ibn al-Anbārī narrated from Abū Dhabyān who said: Ibn ʿAbbās asked us, “Which of the two readings do you consider the frst?” We replied, “The reading of ʿAbdullāh and our reading is the latter.” He said, “The Messenger of God had Gabriel present the Qur’ān to him once every year in the month of Ramaḍān. And in the last year, he presented it to him twice, so ʿAbdullāh witnessed from it what was abrogated and what was changed.”

Comment: This meaning is narrated through other channels from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd himself, and others from the Companions and the Tābiʿūn (Successors). There are other narrations regarding the concept of abrogation.

The essence of what is derived from them is that abrogation can be in ruling, like the abrogated verses that are afrmed in the M uṣḥaf. It might also be in recitation, with its ruling being abrogated or without its ruling being abrogated. It was previously discussed in the interpretation of

His saying: “W hatever verse W e abrogate...” (al-Baqarah:106) and it will be discussed in His saying: “W hen We replace one verse with another...”

(al-Naḥl:101) that the two verses are unrelated to the concept of abrogation in the sense of omitting from recitation. It was also previously mentioned in earlier chapters that these narrations contradict the explicit text of the Qur’ān, so the appropriate course is to associate them with the narrations of alteration and to dismiss both sets entirely.
